title: Digital financial inclusion depends on competitive infrastructure, not access rules alone
source_unit: World Bank, Competition as a Catalyst for Digital Financial Services Usage: Chapeau Paper, September 2026
geography: Comparative case studies of Brazil, Ghana, India, Jamaica, Nigeria, and the Philippines, with global financial-inclusion context

denominator.unit: country case studies: Brazil, Ghana, India, Jamaica, Nigeria, and the Philippines

account_ownership.value: 2025 Global Findex financial-inclusion rates were 89% in India, 86% in Brazil, 81% in Ghana, 63% in Nigeria, and 50% in the Philippines; Jamaica did not participate in the 2024 Findex survey

digital_payments.value: among adults with accounts, 2024 digital-payment usage was 80% in Ghana, 77% in Brazil, 48% in India, 54% in Nigeria, and 40% in the Philippines

access_usage_gap.value: account ownership and active digital-payment use diverge across countries, showing that access to an account does not automatically produce routine digital engagement

mechanism.value: competition, interoperability, market conduct, trust, institutional coordination, and usable last-mile access help determine whether formal access becomes repeated usage

observations.method: Comparative synthesis of six country case studies using 2025 World Bank Global Findex indicators, policy and regulatory review, infrastructure analysis, and stakeholder-informed country research.
observations.uncertainty: The paper explicitly states that it does not establish a causal relationship between competition and digital-finance uptake; countries differ in history, income, infrastructure, measurement, and policy context, and the comparison is not a matched experiment.
observations.subgroup: Low-income and underserved consumers, adults with transaction accounts, small merchants, fintech users, rural and last-mile users, and people who remain formally included but digitally inactive.
observations.counterinterpretation: Digital-payment usage can be constrained by device access, safety, fraud, cash preferences, digital literacy, network reliability, or trust even where competition is present; higher account ownership may still represent meaningful resilience or future option value.

observations.period: 2018-2024; open and interoperable payment infrastructure in Brazil, Ghana, and India

denominator.unit: higher-performing case-study countries: Brazil, Ghana, and India

infrastructure_models.value: Brazil’s Pix, India’s Unified Payments Interface, and Ghana’s Mobile Money Interoperability lowered transaction costs, enabled seamless payments, and supported entry and competition

ghana_interoperability.value: Ghana’s interoperable mobile-money transactions rose from 90,000 to 800,000 within four months after launch; total mobile-money transactions grew from 981.56 million in 2017 to 1.45 billion in 2018

ghana_instant_pay.value: Ghana instant-pay transactions rose from 0.1 million in 2018 to 6.8 million by 2020 after integration with the interoperability framework

india_onboarding.value: the paper reports that Aadhaar-enabled electronic KYC reduced onboarding costs by over 80% in India

mechanism.value: open rails create practical switching and entry possibilities only when access conditions, fees, quality of service, participation rules, and governance prevent the infrastructure from becoming a closed incumbent advantage

observations.method: Comparative case-study analysis of payment systems, digital ID, licensing, open finance, interoperability rules, transaction data, and infrastructure governance.
observations.uncertainty: The reported transaction and onboarding changes are descriptive country examples and are not isolated causal estimates; other reforms, macroeconomic changes, network effects, and adoption dynamics may contribute.
observations.subgroup: Consumers switching between providers, small merchants, fintechs and nonbank providers, rural users reached through agents, and users facing onboarding or transaction-cost barriers.
observations.counterinterpretation: Open infrastructure can create concentration at another layer, generate governance or single-point-of-failure risks, and require safeguards for privacy, cybersecurity, stability, and anti-money-laundering compliance.

observations.period: 2024-2026; competition, trust, and institutional coordination in lower-performing case studies

denominator.unit: mixed- or slower-performance case-study countries: Jamaica, Nigeria, and the Philippines

barriers.value: incumbent market dominance, restricted access to payment infrastructure, limited consent-based data sharing and account mobility, weak sandbox graduation, limited market-conduct supervision, fraud, and low digital literacy are identified as barriers

last_mile.value: Nigeria’s SANEF agent network had enrolled over 1.8 million agents by December 2024, while proposed agent exclusivity could threaten interoperability and last-mile access

trust.value: high fraud rates, weak market-conduct supervision, and low digital literacy can undermine consumer trust and confidence even when accounts and digital rails exist

institutional_design.value: the paper recommends coordinated action among financial, telecommunications, data-protection, competition, and consumer-protection authorities, including fraud detection and dispute resolution

mechanism.value: digital inclusion becomes a trust-and-governance system: access can stall when users cannot switch, contest errors, understand risks, or rely on institutions to police fraud and concentration

observations.method: Country case-study comparison of market structure, agents, payment access, regulatory coordination, fraud, consumer protection, digital literacy, and competition enforcement.
observations.uncertainty: The case-study grouping is comparative and interpretive, not a causal classification; agent counts, trust conditions, usage rates, and institutional arrangements do not by themselves establish welfare effects or universal policy rankings.
observations.subgroup: Consumers with low digital literacy, users exposed to fraud or scams, agents and merchants, nonbank providers, fintech entrants, and consumers dependent on a small number of incumbent platforms.
observations.counterinterpretation: Concentration can sometimes support reliability, investment, or coordinated standards; agent exclusivity may improve oversight in some settings even while risking interoperability in others.

boundary: This record adds a competition-and-interoperability-to-active-digital-use mechanism that extends the prior digital-credit and consumer-protection findings. It is a comparative case-study synthesis, not a causal evaluation, universal country ranking, or direct measure of household welfare; the next test is whether specific infrastructure and governance reforms change switching, transaction costs, fraud exposure, trust, active usage, and distributional access without creating new concentration or single-point-of-failure risks.
